1	# Boldteq Software Factory — Master Overview
2	
3	This document is the single source of truth for the entire Boldteq Software Factory system. If you have lost everything and are starting from scratch, start here, then follow the numbered docs in order.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## What Is This System?
8	
9	The Boldteq Software Factory is a local AI-powered development infrastructure that runs on your Mac. It turns Claude Code (the VS Code extension) from a general-purpose assistant into a coordinated team of 12 specialist agents that know your stack, your standards, and your active projects.
10	
11	Every component in this system has one job. They are designed to work together without requiring you to repeat context.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## The Five Components
16	
17	### 1. Claude Hub — The Control Center
18	
19	**Location:** `/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/`
20	
21	Claude Hub is a local web application running on `http://localhost:3847`. It has two parts:
22	
23	- **Express backend** (`src/server.js`) — REST API that reads/writes agent files, CLAUDE.md files, slash commands, and handles orchestration runs and playground agent calls.
24	- **React/TypeScript/Vite frontend** (`client/`) — The browser dashboard you use to manage everything.
25	
26	Claude Hub is kept alive 24/7 by pm2 and auto-starts on macOS login via a LaunchAgent. You never manually start it.
27	
28	Pages in the dashboard:
29	- **Dashboard** — overview of all projects, agents, and commands
30	- **All Agents** — browse and edit all 12 global agents
31	- **All Commands** — browse slash commands across all projects
32	- **Orchestration** — visual DAG workflow builder for chaining agents
33	- **Playground** — test any single agent interactively
34	- **Global CLAUDE.md** — view and edit the global instruction file
35	- **Project Detail** — per-project agents, commands, and CLAUDE.md
36	- **Setup & Status** — system health, SDK installer, project directories
37	- **Settings** — project directory configuration
38	
39	### 2. Global CLAUDE.md — The Briefing File
40	
41	**Location:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`
42	
43	Every single Claude Code session in every project reads this file first. It contains the Boldteq identity, build standards, agent routing rules, and active project list. It is the foundation that makes Claude Code behave consistently across all projects. Without it, Claude Code has no knowledge of your stack, agents, or standards.
44	
45	### 3. The Agent Roster — The Specialist Team
46	
47	**Location:** `~/.claude/agents/`
48	
49	12 `.md` files, each one a specialist persona with a name, model, and system prompt. Claude Code loads all of them at startup and can route tasks to the right specialist automatically. You can also invoke them explicitly by name. The agents cover the entire build lifecycle from research to deployment to monitoring.
50	
51	### 4. The SDK — Programmatic Agent Access
52	
53	**Location:** `claude-hub/sdk/` (installed as `@boldteq/agents` in each project)
54	
55	A tiny Node.js package that lets any project call any agent over HTTP with one line of code. It posts to Claude Hub which runs `claude -p` with the agent's instructions and streams back the result. Zero cost beyond the existing Claude subscription.
56	
57	### 5. Slash Commands — Repeatable Workflows
58	
59	**Location:** `[project]/.claude/commands/`
60	
61	`.md` files that become `/commandname` shortcuts in Claude Code chat. Pinzo has `/feature`, `/fix`, `/review`, and `/db`. These are pre-written, detailed instructions for the most common workflows in that project. You type the command, pass arguments, and Claude Code executes the full workflow.
62

1	# Claude Hub — Complete Setup Guide
2	
3	This guide walks you through setting up the entire Claude Hub system from zero. By the end, Claude Hub will be running permanently in the background, auto-starting on every login, and all 12 agents will be available in every Claude Code session.
4	
5	If any step fails, jump to the TROUBLESHOOTING section at the bottom.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Prerequisites
10	
11	### Why each prerequisite matters
12	
13	Before installing anything, verify that the right versions are present. The system has been tested and runs on these specific versions. Older versions may work but are not guaranteed.
14	
15	### Node.js 20+
16	
17	Claude Hub's backend is a Node.js Express server. The `@boldteq/agents` SDK uses the native `fetch` API which requires Node 18+. The current setup uses **Node 20.20.1 via nvm**.
18	
19	```bash
20	node --version
21	```
22	
23	Expected output:
24	```
25	v20.20.1
26	```
27	
28	If not installed or wrong version:
29	
30	```bash
31	# Install nvm (Node Version Manager)
32	curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.39.7/install.sh | bash
33	
34	# Reload shell
35	source ~/.zshrc
36	
37	# Install Node 20
38	nvm install 20
39	nvm use 20
40	nvm alias default 20
41	
42	# Verify
43	node --version
44	# v20.x.x
45	```
46	
47	📝 When you install Node via nvm, the binary lives at `~/.nvm/versions/node/v20.x.x/bin/node`. This exact path is used in the LaunchAgent plist. If you change Node versions later, you must update the plist.
48	
49	### npm 9+
50	
51	Ships automatically with Node 18+. Verify:
52	
53	```bash
54	npm --version
55	```
56	
57	Expected output:
58	```
59	10.8.2
60	```
61	
62	No manual installation needed if Node is correct.
63	
64	### pm2 (Process Manager)
65	
66	pm2 keeps Claude Hub running permanently even after closing your terminal. It restarts the process if it crashes, and persists the process list across reboots.
67	
68	```bash
69	npm install -g pm2
70	pm2 --version
71	```
72	
73	Expected output:
74	```
75	6.0.14
76	```
77	
78	If not installed:
79	```bash
80	npm install -g pm2
81	```
82	
83	📝 The `-g` flag installs pm2 globally so it's accessible from any directory and as a system command.
84	
85	### Claude Code (CLI)
86	
87	Claude Hub calls the `claude` CLI to run agents. This must be installed and authenticated.
88	
89	```bash
90	claude --version
91	```
92	
93	Expected output (something like):
94	```
95	Claude Code 1.x.x
96	```
97	
98	If not installed, go to https://claude.ai/code and follow the installation instructions. After installing, authenticate:
99	
100	```bash
101	claude login
102	```
103	
104	⚠️ Claude Hub will not be able to run agents (Playground, Orchestration) if `claude` is not authenticated. The dashboard itself will still work.
105	
106	---

108	## Step 1 — Verify the Claude Hub Directory
109	
110	Why this matters: Claude Hub must live at a specific absolute path because that path is hardcoded in `ecosystem.config.js` and the LaunchAgent plist. Moving it after setup requires updating those files.
111	
112	```bash
113	ls "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/"
114	```
115	
116	Expected output:
117	```
118	IMPLEMENTATION_CHECKLIST.md
119	ORCHESTRATION_GUIDE.md
120	README.md
121	client/
122	config.json
123	docs/
124	ecosystem.config.js
125	node_modules/
126	orchestrations.json
127	package.json
128	package-lock.json
129	public/
130	public-dist/
131	sdk/
132	src/
133	```

135	Key files to confirm exist:
136	- `src/server.js` — the backend
137	- `ecosystem.config.js` — pm2 configuration
138	- `sdk/` — the @boldteq/agents package
139	- `client/` — the React frontend source
140	- `public-dist/` — the built frontend (served by Express)
141	
142	⚠️ If `public-dist/` is missing or empty, the frontend won't load. See Step 3 for how to build it.
143	
144	### Checking ecosystem.config.js
145	
146	This file tells pm2 how to run Claude Hub. Read it:
147	
148	```bash
149	cat "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/ecosystem.config.js"
150	```
151	
152	Expected content:
153	```javascript
154	module.exports = {
155	  apps: [
156	    {
157	      name: 'claude-hub',
158	      script: './src/server.js',
159	      cwd: '/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub',
160	      interpreter: 'node',
161	      watch: false,
162	      autorestart: true,
163	      max_restarts: 5,
164	      env: {
165	        NODE_ENV: 'production',
166	        PORT: 3847,
167	      },
168	      error_file: '/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-error.log',
169	      out_file: '/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-out.log',
170	      log_date_format: 'YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss',
171	    },
172	  ],
173	}
174	```
175	
176	Each field explained:
177	- `name: 'claude-hub'` — the pm2 process name. Used in all pm2 commands.
178	- `script: './src/server.js'` — the entry point, relative to `cwd`.

183	- `PORT: 3847` — Claude Hub listens on this port. All SDK calls and browser access use this port.
184	- `error_file` / `out_file` — log files. View with `pm2 logs claude-hub`.
185	
186	⚠️ If you are on a different Mac or different username, update the `cwd` path to match your actual home directory.

378	## Step 5 — LaunchAgent Setup (Auto-Start on macOS Login)
379	
380	### Why a LaunchAgent?
381	
382	pm2 manages the process, but pm2 itself needs to be started after a reboot. The LaunchAgent is macOS's built-in service system. It runs a specified program when you log in, before you open any apps.
383	
384	Without a LaunchAgent:
385	- After a Mac restart, pm2 is not running
386	- Claude Hub is not running
387	- The SDK fails silently in all projects
388	- You must manually run `pm2 resurrect` or `pm2 start ecosystem.config.js` after every reboot
389	
390	With the LaunchAgent:
391	- Mac restarts → login → LaunchAgent fires → `node src/server.js` starts → Claude Hub is running → all SDK calls work
392	
393	📝 Note: The LaunchAgent in this setup runs Claude Hub **directly** (not via pm2). This is intentional — it guarantees Claude Hub starts even if pm2's process list was lost.
394	
395	### Check if the plist already exists
396	
397	```bash
398	ls ~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.boldteq.claude-hub.plist
399	```
400	
401	Expected: path printed (file exists).
402	
403	If missing, you need to create it. See "Creating the plist from scratch" below.
404	
405	### The full plist content
406	
407	The file at `~/Library/LaunchAgents/io.boldteq.claude-hub.plist` should contain:
408	
409	```xml
410	<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
411	<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
412	<plist version="1.0">
413	<dict>
414	  <key>Label</key>
415	  <string>io.boldteq.claude-hub</string>
416	
417	  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
418	  <array>
419	    <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.1/bin/node</string>
420	    <string>/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/src/server.js</string>
421	  </array>
422	
423	  <key>WorkingDirectory</key>
424	  <string>/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub</string>
425	
426	  <key>RunAtLoad</key>
427	  <true/>
428	
429	  <key>KeepAlive</key>
430	  <true/>
431	
432	  <key>StandardOutPath</key>
433	  <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-launchd.log</string>
434	
435	  <key>StandardErrorPath</key>
436	  <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.pm2/logs/claude-hub-launchd-error.log</string>
437	
438	  <key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
439	  <dict>
440	    <key>PORT</key>
441	    <string>3847</string>
442	    <key>PATH</key>
443	    <string>/Users/yashbaldha/.nvm/versions/node/v20.20.1/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin</string>

449	Each key explained:
450	- `Label` — unique identifier for this LaunchAgent. Used with `launchctl`.
451	- `ProgramArguments` — the exact command to run. First element is the Node binary path, second is the script. Must use absolute paths.

454	- `KeepAlive: true` — macOS will restart the process if it exits. Like pm2's autorestart.
455	- `StandardOutPath` / `StandardErrorPath` — log files. Reuses the pm2 log directory for convenience.

565	```

567	The current setup uses the LaunchAgent as the authoritative runner (port 3847), and pm2 for convenience commands and log streaming.

2	
3	This document covers everything about the 12 global agents: what they are, how Claude Code discovers them, how to invoke them, how to create new ones, and how to maintain them.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## What Are Agents?
8	
9	An agent is a `.md` file with YAML frontmatter that defines a specialist persona for Claude Code. When Claude Code runs an agent, it reads the file's frontmatter for metadata and uses the file body as the system prompt for that Claude call.
10	
11	Agents solve a specific problem: instead of explaining your entire stack and standards to Claude on every task, you write that context once in the agent file. From then on, invoking `koda` means "use this pre-loaded context about our Shopify stack and feature-building standards."
12	
13	They also allow automatic routing — Claude Code reads all agent `description` fields and can route a task to the right specialist without you explicitly naming one.
14	
15	---
16	
17	## How Claude Code Discovers Agents
18	
19	Claude Code reads all `.md` files in these directories at startup:
20	
21	1. `~/.claude/agents/` — global agents, available in every project
22	2. `[project]/.claude/agents/` — project-level agents, available only in that project
23	
24	No registration or configuration needed. Drop a `.md` file into either directory and it is immediately available in the next Claude Code session.
25	
26	📝 Claude Code loads agents at session start, not on every message. If you create or edit an agent file, open a new chat window to pick up the changes.
27	
28	### File Naming
29	
30	The filename (without `.md`) becomes the agent's slug — the name you use to call it programmatically:
31	- `koda.md` → invoked as `koda`
32	- `nova.md` → invoked as `nova`
33	- `custom-specialist.md` → invoked as `custom-specialist`
34	
35	Names must match the regex `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+`. No spaces, no special characters.
36	
37	### Global vs Project-Level Agents
38	
39	| Scope | Directory | Available in |
40	|-------|-----------|-------------|
41	| Global | `~/.claude/agents/` | Every Claude Code session, every project |
42	| Project | `[project]/.claude/agents/` | Only when that project is open |
43	
44	Project-level agents override global agents with the same filename. If `~/.claude/agents/koda.md` and `Pinzo/.claude/agents/koda.md` both exist, Pinzo's version takes priority when working in Pinzo. This lets you specialize a global agent for one project without affecting others.
45	
46	**When to use project-level agents:**
47	- A workflow is too specific to one project to belong globally (e.g., a Pinzo widget specialist)
48	- You want to override a global agent with project-specific context
49	- A project has a unique tech stack that doesn't apply anywhere else
50	
51	**When to keep it global:**
52	- The agent's skills apply to all projects (most agents should be global)
53	- You want Rex to be able to route to this agent from any project

334	## How to Create a New Agent
335	
336	### When to create a new global agent
337	
338	- You have a recurring specialist role that cuts across multiple projects (e.g., a data migration specialist, a Stripe billing expert)
339	- The specialist's context is too long to re-explain in every prompt
340	- You want Claude Code to auto-route to this specialist
341	
342	### When to create a project-level agent instead
343	
344	- The specialist is deeply tied to one project (e.g., Pinzo's widget specialist who knows the exact storefront widget API)
345	- The agent uses project-specific file paths, model names, or business logic
346	- You want to override a global agent's behavior for one project
347	
348	### The agent file format
349	
350	```markdown
351	---
352	name: Agent Display Name
353	description: What this agent does. Be specific — Claude Code uses this to auto-route tasks.
354	model: sonnet
355	tools: Read,Write,Edit,Bash,Glob,Grep
356	---
357	
358	Your agent's system prompt goes here.
359	
360	## Identity
361	Who this agent is. Give it a name and a role.
362	"You are [Name], the [role] for the Boldteq Software Factory."
363	
364	## Responsibilities
365	Exactly what this agent does. Be explicit.
366	- Does X
367	- Does Y
368	- Does NOT do Z (important — define scope boundaries)
369	
370	## Standards
371	What quality standards apply to this agent's output.
372	
373	## Patterns to Use
374	Concrete patterns this agent should always apply.
375	
376	## Patterns to Avoid
377	Antipatterns this agent should never repeat.
378	
379	## Output Format
380	How this agent should structure its responses.
381	```
382	
383	### Frontmatter fields
384	
385	| Field | Required | Values | Notes |
386	|-------|----------|--------|-------|
387	| `name` | Yes | Any string | Shown in Claude Hub UI |
388	| `description` | Yes | Any string | Used for auto-routing — be precise |
389	| `model` | Yes | `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku` | Affects cost and quality |
390	| `tools` | No | Comma-separated tool names | Restricts available tools |
391	
392	### Model selection guide
393	
394	| Model | Speed | Cost | Use for |
395	|-------|-------|------|---------|
396	| `haiku` | Fastest | Lowest | Simple tasks: formatting, classification, simple transforms |
397	| `sonnet` | Fast | Medium | Most agents — code generation, research, content writing |
398	| `opus` | Slowest | Highest | Complex reasoning — architecture decisions, orchestration, deep code review |
399	
400	Use `opus` only for Rex, Arya, and Sage. Everything else uses `sonnet`. The cost difference is significant when running many agent calls.
401	
402	### How to write a good description (for auto-routing)
403	
404	The `description` field is what Claude Code reads to decide which agent handles a task. Bad descriptions lead to wrong routing.
405	
406	**Bad description:**
407	```
408	description: Helps with code and stuff
409	```
410	
411	**Good description:**
412	```
413	description: Shopify app bug fixer. Diagnoses and fixes errors in Remix/React Router apps: TypeScript errors, Prisma DB issues, Shopify auth failures, webhook bugs, billing errors. Has category-based diagnostic playbook.
414	```
415	
416	The good description includes: what it does, in what context, what kinds of tasks, and any notable specializations.
417

485	## Agent Quality Tips
486	
487	### What makes agent instructions good
488	
489	1. **Clear identity** — the agent knows exactly who it is and what its scope is
490	2. **Explicit non-responsibilities** — saying "you do NOT write tests" is as important as saying what it does do
491	3. **Concrete patterns** — "use `upsert` for singleton records" beats "handle data correctly"
492	4. **Output format specified** — the agent knows what shape to return results in
493	5. **Quality gates explicit** — the agent knows what "done" means
494	
495	### What makes agent instructions bad
496	
497	1. **Too broad** — "help with any code task" gives no routing signal
498	2. **Missing context** — agent doesn't know the stack, framework versions, or project structure
499	3. **No scope boundary** — agent will attempt everything instead of knowing when to hand off
500	4. **Ambiguous instructions** — "handle errors properly" vs "wrap every action in try/catch and return `{ error: msg }` with status 500"
501	5. **No output format** — agent returns different structures on every call
502	
503	### The "one clear responsibility" rule
504	
505	Each agent should be able to answer "what is the one thing you are the expert on?" in one sentence. If the answer requires "and also...", split into multiple agents or make the description more specific.
506	
507	Koda builds features. Vex fixes bugs. Luna tests. Sage reviews. They do not step on each other's territory because their scope boundaries are explicit in their files.

1	# @boldteq/agents SDK — Complete Reference
2	
3	This document covers the `@boldteq/agents` SDK: what it is, how it works internally, how to install it in a new project, and the full API reference with examples.
4	
5	---
6	
7	## What the SDK Is and the Problem It Solves
8	
9	Every Boldteq project occasionally needs to call a Claude agent programmatically — not just interactively from a chat window. Examples:
10	
11	- An API route in Rankora that calls Quill to generate a job description summary
12	- A Pinzo webhook handler that calls Vex to diagnose an error and log the diagnosis
13	- A build script that calls Nova to research a competitor before a planning session
14	- An admin dashboard action that calls Koda to auto-generate code suggestions
15	
16	Without the SDK, doing this requires: knowing the `claude` CLI syntax, managing subprocesses, parsing SSE output, handling timeouts, and writing error handling from scratch — every time, in every project.
17	
18	The SDK wraps all of that into a single function:
19	
20	```javascript
21	const result = await callAgent('quill', 'Write App Store listing for Pinzo')
22	```
23	
24	That's it. One line. The SDK handles the HTTP call to Claude Hub, which handles the `claude -p` subprocess, SSE streaming, and response parsing. The result comes back as a structured object.
25	
26	---
27	
28	## Architecture: How a Call Actually Works
29	
30	```
31	Your code calls:
32	callAgent('quill', 'Write listing for Pinzo')
33	  │
34	  ▼
35	SDK (sdk/index.js)
36	  POST http://localhost:3847/api/playground/run
37	  Body: { agentName: 'quill', prompt: 'Write listing...' }
38	  │
39	  ▼
40	Claude Hub backend (src/server.js)
41	  1. Reads ~/.claude/agents/quill.md
42	  2. Extracts the agent's system prompt (body after frontmatter)
43	  3. Constructs: claude -p "[system prompt]\n\n[user prompt]"
44	  4. Spawns the subprocess
45	  5. Streams output back as Server-Sent Events (SSE)
46	  │
47	  ▼
48	SDK parses the SSE stream:
49	  - Looks for { type: 'done', output: '...' }
50	  - Or { type: 'error', error: '...' }
51	  │
52	  ▼
53	Returns to your code:
54	  { success: true, output: '...the agent response...', agent: 'quill' }
55	  or
56	  { success: false, output: '', agent: 'quill', error: 'reason' }
57	```
58	
59	Key characteristics:
60	- **Zero additional cost** — uses your existing Claude subscription. The `claude -p` subprocess runs under the same authenticated account as your interactive Claude Code sessions.
61	- **Synchronous from your code's perspective** — `await callAgent(...)` blocks until the agent completes or times out.
62	- **Never throws** — the SDK catches all errors internally and returns them in the `error` field. Your code never needs a try/catch around `callAgent`.
63	- **Requires Claude Hub running** — if `http://localhost:3847` is not reachable, the call fails immediately with a "not reachable" error message.

209	 * @boldteq/agents
210	 * Call any global Claude agent from any Boldteq app.
211	 * Claude Hub must be running (auto-starts on login via LaunchAgent).
212	 */
213	
214	const CLAUDE_HUB_URL = process.env.CLAUDE_HUB_URL || 'http://localhost:3847'

216	/**
217	 * Call a global agent with a prompt.
218	 * @param {string} agentName - e.g. "quill", "vex", "nova", "sage", "koda"
219	 * @param {string} prompt - the task to send
220	 * @param {number} [timeoutMs=120000] - timeout in ms
221	 * @returns {Promise<{ success: boolean, output: string, agent: string, error?: string }>}
222	 */
223	async function callAgent(agentName, prompt, timeoutMs = 120000) {
224	  const controller = new AbortController()
225	  const timeout = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), timeoutMs)
226	
227	  try {
228	    const response = await fetch(`${CLAUDE_HUB_URL}/api/playground/run`, {
229	      method: 'POST',
230	      headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
231	      body: JSON.stringify({ agentName, prompt }),
232	      signal: controller.signal,
233	    })
234	
235	    clearTimeout(timeout)
236	
237	    if (!response.ok) {
238	      throw new Error(`Claude Hub returned ${response.status}`)
239	    }
240	
241	    const text = await response.text()
242	    const events = text
243	      .split('\n')
244	      .filter(line => line.startsWith('data: '))
245	      .map(line => { try { return JSON.parse(line.slice(6)) } catch { return null } })
246	      .filter(Boolean)
247	
248	    const errorEvent = events.find(e => e.type === 'error')
249	    if (errorEvent) return { success: false, output: '', agent: agentName, error: errorEvent.error }
250	
251	    const doneEvent = events.find(e => e.type === 'done' || e.type === 'complete')
252	    return { success: true, output: doneEvent?.output || '', agent: agentName }
253	
254	  } catch (err) {
255	    clearTimeout(timeout)
256	    const msg = err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)
257	    return {
258	      success: false,
259	      output: '',
260	      agent: agentName,
261	      error: msg.includes('abort')
262	        ? `Timed out after ${timeoutMs / 1000}s`
263	        : `Claude Hub not reachable at ${CLAUDE_HUB_URL} — is it running?`,
264	    }
265	  }
266	}

292	  }

339	## Full API Reference
340	
341	### `callAgent(agentName, prompt, timeoutMs?)`
342	
343	The primary function. Calls any global agent with a task and waits for the response.
344	
345	**Parameters:**
346	
347	| Parameter | Type | Required | Default | Description |
348	|-----------|------|----------|---------|-------------|
349	| `agentName` | `string` | Yes | — | Agent filename without `.md`. Must match a file in `~/.claude/agents/`. Example: `'koda'`, `'quill'`, `'nova'` |
350	| `prompt` | `string` | Yes | — | The task or instruction to send to the agent. Write it as you would write a message to that specialist. |
351	| `timeoutMs` | `number` | No | `120000` | Maximum time to wait in milliseconds. Default is 2 minutes. Increase for complex tasks. |
352	
353	**Returns:** `Promise<AgentResult>`
354	
355	```typescript
356	interface AgentResult {
357	  success: boolean   // true if the agent ran and returned output
358	  output: string     // the agent's full response text (empty string if success is false)
359	  agent: string      // the agentName that was called (echoed back)
360	  error?: string     // error message (only set if success is false)
361	}
362	```
363	
364	**Examples:**
365	
366	```javascript
367	// Basic call
368	const result = await callAgent('quill', 'Write a tagline for Pinzo')
369	if (result.success) {
370	  console.log(result.output)
371	} else {
372	  console.error(result.error)
373	}
374	
375	// With custom timeout for a long task
376	const result = await callAgent(
377	  'koda',
378	  'Build the complete subscription billing page with plan comparison',
379	  300000  // 5 minutes
380	)
381	
382	// Fire and forget (don't await the result)
383	callAgent('mira', 'Extract lessons from today\'s Pinzo session')
384	```
385	
386	**Error scenarios:**
387	
388	The `success: false` result happens when:
389	1. Claude Hub is not reachable: `error` will be "Claude Hub not reachable at http://localhost:3847 — is it running?"
390	2. The call times out: `error` will be "Timed out after Xs"
391	3. Claude Hub returns a non-200 HTTP status
392	4. The `claude` CLI subprocess fails or returns an error event
393

396	### `listAgents()`
397	
398	Fetches all available global agents from Claude Hub.
399	
400	**Returns:** `Promise<Agent[]>`
401	
402	```typescript
403	interface Agent {
404	  filename: string    // filename without .md, e.g. 'koda'
405	  name: string        // display name from frontmatter, e.g. 'Koda — Feature Builder'
406	  description: string // description from frontmatter
407	  model: string       // 'sonnet', 'opus', or 'haiku'

420	})

423	// arya (opus): Stack selection, data model design, sprint planning...

425	// koda (sonnet): All production code — frontend, backend, database...

433	### `isOnline()`
434	
435	Checks if Claude Hub is reachable. Uses a 3-second timeout to avoid blocking.
436	
437	**Returns:** `Promise<boolean>`
438	
439	`true` if Claude Hub responds to `GET /api/global/agents` with a 200 status.
440	`false` if the request fails, times out, or returns a non-200 status.
441	
442	**Example:**
443	
444	```javascript
445	import { isOnline, callAgent } from '@boldteq/agents'
446	
447	async function generateCopy(product: string) {
448	  if (!await isOnline()) {
449	    throw new Error('Claude Hub is offline. Start it with: pm2 start claude-hub')
450	  }
451	  return await callAgent('quill', `Write a tagline for ${product}`)
452	}
453	```
454	
455	Use `isOnline()` as a guard when Claude Hub being offline would cause a bad user experience (e.g., a UI action that depends on agent output). For fire-and-forget calls (logging, async enrichment), just call the agent directly and handle the error in the result.

1	# Slash Commands — Complete Reference
2	
3	This document covers everything about slash commands: what they are, how Claude Code discovers them, the `$ARGUMENTS` system, Pinzo's four commands in detail, and how to create new commands for any project.

6	
7	## What Are Slash Commands?
8	
9	Slash commands are `.md` files stored in `[project]/.claude/commands/`. When you type `/commandname` in Claude Code chat, it reads that file and executes its content as a prompt — with `$ARGUMENTS` replaced by whatever text follows the command name.
10	
11	They are project-scoped workflow shortcuts. Instead of writing out the same detailed instructions every time you want to build a feature or run a review, you write them once in a command file and invoke them in one line.
12	
13	### Example
14	
15	Without a slash command:
16	> "Build a complete feature for Pinzo. Read CLAUDE.md first. Check Prisma schema. Handle auth. Use Polaris v13. Add empty states and loading states. Include Toast feedback for every mutation. Run typecheck when done. Report what was changed."
17	
18	With a slash command:
19	> `/feature Add ZIP code import from CSV`
20	
21	Same instructions, one line.
22	
23	---
24	
25	## How Slash Commands Differ from Agents
26	
27	| | Agents | Slash Commands |
28	|-|--------|----------------|
29	| **Location** | `~/.claude/agents/` or `[project]/.claude/agents/` | `[project]/.claude/commands/` |
30	| **Scope** | Global or project | Project-only, always |
31	| **Invoked by** | Claude Code auto-routing, `@name`, SDK | You typing `/commandname` |
32	| **Has identity?** | Yes — name, model, description, persona | No — just instructions |
33	| **Purpose** | Specialist persona with persistent expertise | Repeatable workflow for one project |
34	| **Arguments?** | No — you describe the task in full | Yes — `$ARGUMENTS` placeholder |
35	| **Cost** | Uses agent's configured model | Uses current session model |
36	
37	**Rule of thumb:**
38	- Use agents when you need Claude Code to automatically know about a specialist (Rex, Koda, Vex, etc.)
39	- Use slash commands for project-specific workflows you run manually and repeatedly (build feature, fix bug, run migration)

186	### `/review` — Quality Gate Before Shipping

188	**File:** `Pinzo/.claude/commands/review.md`

198	Checks for: auth missing on admin routes, cross-shop data leaks (queries without `where: { shop: session.shop }`), public routes with accidental admin auth, exposed secrets in API responses, unsanitized input on public endpoints, missing CORS headers.

201	Checks for: Shopify API calls in components (must be in loaders/actions), raw fetch for Shopify API (must use `admin.graphql()`), missing idempotency in webhooks, raw HTML layout elements, missing loading/empty states/Toast feedback, ungated premium features.

204	Checks for: TypeScript `any`, `console.log` in production code, TODO/FIXME comments, hardcoded values, wrong Remix imports, missing error handling.

206	**Phase 5 — API contract validation:**
207	If public APIs changed: verifies response shapes, status codes, CORS headers, and shop parameter validation.

214	/review src/routes/app.zip-codes.tsx

292	- Lowercase only: `feature`, `fix`, `review`, `db`

302	- What quality gates must pass before the task is "done"
303	- What the output/report format should be

395	## Commands vs Agents: Decision Guide
396	
397	| Situation | Use |
398	|-----------|-----|
399	| You do the same workflow in this project more than once a week | Slash command |
400	| The workflow is always the same but the subject changes | Slash command with `$ARGUMENTS` |
401	| You need Claude Code to automatically route to a specialist | Agent |
402	| The specialist's expertise spans multiple projects | Global agent |
403	| The specialist is deeply tied to one project's code | Project agent |
404	| You want to invoke logic programmatically from Node code | Agent via SDK |
405	| You want to invoke it from the chat interface by typing | Slash command |
406

2	
3	This document covers everything about the Orchestration feature in Claude Hub: what it is, when to use it, how to build pipelines, the execution engine, advanced patterns, and troubleshooting.

5	---
6	
7	## What Is Orchestration?
8	
9	Orchestration is a visual workflow system inside Claude Hub that lets you chain multiple Claude agents together as a directed graph (DAG). Each node in the graph runs one agent or custom step. The output of each node automatically flows into the next node as context.
10	
11	You define the pipeline once. Then you give it a top-level task and run it. Each agent handles one stage: researching, planning, building, reviewing. The whole pipeline executes without you manually passing output from one agent to the next.
12	
13	### The simplest possible orchestration
14	
15	```
16	[Task Input] → Nova (research) → Quill (draft)
17	```
18	
19	1. You type: "Write App Store listing for Pinzo"
20	2. Nova researches Pinzo and similar apps, returns competitor analysis and key angles
21	3. Quill receives Nova's research as context and writes the App Store listing using it
22	
23	Nova's output becomes Quill's input automatically. You didn't have to copy-paste anything.
24	
25	---
26	
27	## When to Use Orchestration vs Other Approaches
28	
29	| Situation | Best approach |
30	|-----------|--------------|
31	| Quick one-off task | Ask Claude Code directly in chat |
32	| Repeatable single-agent workflow | Slash command |
33	| Multi-step task with distinct specialist phases | Orchestration |
34	| Task where later stages need earlier stages' output | Orchestration |
35	| You want to test different pipeline structures | Orchestration |
36	| Programmatic agent calls from code | SDK (`callAgent`) |
37	| Interactive back-and-forth conversation | Claude Code chat |
38	
39	Orchestration is best when you have 2+ stages that require different expertise and where later stages genuinely benefit from earlier stages' output. If all stages can be done by one agent or don't need context from each other, use a slash command instead.

43	## How the Visual Canvas Works
44	
45	### Opening Orchestration
46	
47	1. Open http://localhost:3847
48	2. Click **Orchestration** in the left sidebar
49	
50	You land on the canvas. It has:
51	- A blank canvas area (main working area)
52	- A sidebar on the right for node configuration
53	- A Run panel at the bottom
54	- A toolbar at the top with: New, Save, templates, node palette
55	
56	### Nodes
57	
58	Every pipeline is made of nodes. Each node represents one step.
59	
60	**Node types:**
61	
62	| Type | Description | Claude call? |
63	|------|-------------|-------------|
64	| Start / Task Input | The initial prompt. Pass-through — no agent runs. | No |
65	| Agent Node | Runs a global agent (Nova, Quill, Koda, etc.) with an optional instruction override | Yes |
66	| Custom Step | Runs Claude with instructions you write entirely yourself | Yes |
67	
68	**Node anatomy:**
69	- **Label** — the display name on the canvas (e.g., "Research", "Draft", "Polish")
70	- **Agent** (Agent nodes only) — which agent from `~/.claude/agents/` to use
71	- **Instructions** — what to tell this agent/step. This overrides or supplements the agent's default behavior for this specific step.
72	
73	### Edges
74	
75	Edges are arrows connecting nodes. They define the flow:
76	- Draw an arrow from Node A to Node B → Node B receives Node A's output as context
77	- Draw multiple arrows into Node B → Node B receives all upstream outputs, labeled by source
78	- A node with no incoming edges starts with the original task as its context
79	
80	### The DAG constraint
81	
82	The graph must be a DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) — no cycles. You cannot connect Node C back to Node A if A → B → C. The execution engine uses topological sort, which requires no cycles. If you add a circular edge, the system rejects it.
83	
84	Valid graphs:
85	```
86	Linear:      A → B → C
87	Fan-out:     A → B
88	             A → C
89	Fan-in:      B → D
90	             C → D
91	Combined:    A → B → D → E
92	             A → C → D
93	```
94	
95	---
96	
97	## The Execution Engine
98	
99	### What happens when you click Run
100	
101	**Phase 1 — Graph validation:**
102	- Receives the node list and edge list from the frontend
103	- Builds a node map for fast lookup
104	- Detects cycles (rejects if found)
105	- Performs topological sort to determine execution order
106	- Ensures dependencies are respected (no node runs before its inputs are ready)
107	
108	**Phase 2 — Load agents:**
109	- Reads all `.md` files from `~/.claude/agents/`
110	- Reads `.md` files from each project's `.claude/agents/`
111	- Builds a map: agentName → full system prompt
112	
113	**Phase 3 — Sequential execution:**
114	
115	For each node in topological order:
116	
117	1. If it's a start/task node: store the original task as its output, emit `{ type: 'start' }` + `{ type: 'done' }` events, move on. No Claude call made.
118	
119	2. If it's an agent or custom node:
120	   - Emit `{ type: 'start', nodeId, label }` → the canvas shows this node as "running" (purple animation)
121	   - Collect outputs from all upstream nodes
122	   - Build context string:
123	     ```
124	     ## Output from [Upstream Node A label]:
125	     [Node A's output]
126	     
127	     ## Output from [Upstream Node B label]:
128	     [Node B's output]
129	     ```
130	   - Build full prompt:
131	     ```
132	     [Agent system prompt or custom instructions]
133	     
134	     ---
135	     
136	     [Context from upstream nodes]
137	     
138	     Provide your response:
139	     ```
140	   - Run `claude -p "[full prompt]"` as a subprocess
141	   - Wait for subprocess to complete (120-second timeout)
142	   - Store the output
143	   - Emit `{ type: 'done', nodeId, label, output }` → canvas shows green checkmark
144	
145	3. After all nodes: emit `{ type: 'complete', finalOutput }` → Run panel shows final result
146	
147	**Phase 4 — SSE streaming:**
148	
149	The frontend receives real-time updates via Server-Sent Events. The node statuses change live as execution proceeds:
150	- `idle` → gray (before run)
151	- `running` → animated purple (executing now)
152	- `done` → green with checkmark
153	- `error` → red with error icon

157	## Context Passing: How Upstream Outputs Become Downstream Inputs
158	
159	This is the key mechanism. Understanding it helps you write better pipelines.
160	
161	### Single upstream (linear chain)
162	
163	Node B receives output from Node A:
164	
165	```
166	Full prompt sent to Node B:
167	═══════════════════════════════
168	[Node B's instructions]
169	
170	---
171	
172	## Output from Research:
173	[Everything Nova returned]
174	
175	Provide your response:
176	═══════════════════════════════
177	```
178	
179	Node B's Claude call sees Node A's full output as context. It can reference, summarize, or build on it.
180	
181	### Multiple upstream (fan-in)
182	
183	Node D receives from both Node B and Node C:
184	
185	```
186	Full prompt sent to Node D:
187	═══════════════════════════════
188	[Node D's instructions]
189	
190	---
191	
192	## Output from Planner:
193	[Everything the Planner node returned]
194	
195	## Output from Researcher:
196	[Everything the Researcher node returned]
197	
198	Provide your response:
199	═══════════════════════════════
200	```
201	
202	Node D's Claude call sees both outputs, clearly labeled. It can synthesize them, compare them, or use them independently.

314	## Node Instructions: Bad vs Good
315	
316	This is the most important thing to get right. Bad node instructions produce bad or empty output.
317	
318	### The root problem
319	
320	If node instructions say "analyze this" without specifying what to produce, Claude might:
321	- Ask clarifying questions instead of producing output
322	- Return a meta-commentary about what it would do, rather than doing it
323	- Produce the right content but buried in unnecessary explanation
324	
325	**Bad node instructions:**
326	```
327	Analyze the research and think about what content would work best.
328	```
329	Claude will describe what good content looks like, not write it.
330	
331	**Good node instructions:**
332	```
333	You are a Shopify app copywriter. Using the research provided:
334	1. Identify the top 3 user pain points mentioned
335	2. Write a 5-bullet feature list that directly addresses those pain points
336	3. Write a 150-word app description
337	
338	Return the bullets and description only. No commentary.
339	```
340	Claude has a clear role, a clear input, clear output requirements, and explicit format.
341	
342	### The explicit output format rule
343	
344	Every node instruction should specify:
345	1. **What format to return** ("Return a bullet list", "Return only the code", "Return a structured JSON object")
346	2. **What NOT to include** ("No commentary", "No preamble", "No explanation")
347	3. **Length or scope** ("150 words", "5 bullets", "complete implementation")
348	
349	Without these, agents often return meta-content (explaining what they're doing) rather than the deliverable itself.
350	
351	### More examples
352	
353	**Bad — Planner node:**
354	```
355	Think about the task and break it down.
356	```
357	
358	**Good — Planner node:**
359	```
360	Break the given task into 5 or fewer concrete implementation steps.
361	Number each step. Be specific: mention file names, method names, and data types where relevant.
362	Return the numbered list only.
363	```
364	
365	**Bad — Code reviewer:**
366	```
367	Review the code.
368	```
369	
370	**Good — Code reviewer:**
371	```
372	You are a TypeScript code reviewer.
373	Check for:
374	1. Missing type annotations
375	2. Unsafe type assertions or `any` usage
376	3. Unhandled promise rejections
377	4. Missing error boundaries
378	
379	Output format:
380	## Issues Found
381	- [severity: critical/warning] [file/line]: [problem] → [fix]
382	
383	## Verdict: PASS / NEEDS FIXES
384	```

420	## Advanced Patterns
421	
422	### Pattern 1: Fan-Out (Multi-Perspective Research)
423	
424	Use when you want multiple independent perspectives on the same topic before synthesizing.
425	
426	```
427	Task Input
428	  → Researcher A: "Find solutions in TypeScript/Node"
429	  → Researcher B: "Find solutions in Python approaches"
430	  → Synthesizer: "Compare approaches, recommend best for our stack"
431	  → Developer: "Implement the recommended approach"
432	```
433	
434	Both Researcher A and B receive only the task. Synthesizer receives both their outputs. Developer receives Synthesizer's recommendation.
435	
436	**When to use:** Architecture decisions, technical comparisons, multi-angle analysis.
437	
438	### Pattern 2: Plan → Implement → Validate
439	
440	A three-stage code generation pipeline.
441	
442	```
443	Task Input → Planner (Arya) → Developer (Koda) → Reviewer (Sage)
444	```
445	
446	Arya breaks the task into a build plan. Koda implements from the plan. Sage reviews Koda's implementation.
447	
448	**When to use:** Complex feature builds where you want architecture thought through before coding.
449	
450	### Pattern 3: Summarizer Nodes for Long Context
451	
452	Problem: Node 1 outputs 8KB of research. Node 2 outputs 12KB of code. Node 3 receives 20KB of context — slow, expensive, risks hitting limits.
453	
454	Solution: Add a Summarizer node between steps.
455	
456	```
457	Research → Summarizer (100 words max) → Developer
458	```
459	
460	Summarizer instruction:
461	```
462	Condense the above research into 5 key bullet points. 
463	Maximum 100 words total. 
464	Preserve the most actionable insights.
465	```
466	
467	The Developer then works with 100 words of targeted context instead of 8KB of raw research.
468	
469	### Pattern 4: Cascading Specialization
470	
471	```
472	Task (general) → Planner (breaks into sub-tasks) → Specialist A (sub-task 1) → Specialist B (sub-task 2) → Integrator (combines)
473	```
474	
475	Each specialist receives: the original task + Planner's output + their specific part to handle.
476	The Integrator receives: all specialist outputs and synthesizes them.
477	
478	**When to use:** Building multiple distinct components that need to work together. Example: "Build the pricing page" → Planner splits into (a) pricing logic, (b) UI layout, (c) copy. Koda handles logic and layout in parallel (conceptually). Quill handles copy. Final node integrates.
479	
480	### Pattern 5: Validation Gate
481	
482	```
483	Task → Developer → Validator → (done if valid, re-run with feedback if not)
484	```
485	
486	Validator instruction:
487	```
488	Review the code above. Check:
489	1. Does it compile? (TypeScript syntax check)
490	2. Does it follow the project patterns?
491	3. Are error handling and loading states present?
492	
493	Output:
494	## PASS / FAIL
495	If FAIL, list: [issue] → [required fix]
496	```
497	
498	If Validator outputs FAIL, you can see exactly what needs fixing and re-run with adjusted Developer instructions that address the Validator's feedback.
499

501	
502	## Performance Considerations
503	
504	### Timing
505	
506	| Operation | Typical time |
507	|-----------|-------------|
508	| Start/Task node | < 1ms (no Claude call) |
509	| Simple agent step (short task) | 5–20 seconds |
510	| Complex agent step (full implementation) | 20–60 seconds |
511	| Full 3-node pipeline | 30–90 seconds |
512	| Full 5-node pipeline | 75–180 seconds |
513	
514	Every node makes exactly one `claude -p` subprocess call. Nodes execute sequentially — not in parallel.
515	
516	### How to keep pipelines fast
517	
518	1. **Limit context size** — use summarizer nodes between heavy output nodes
519	2. **Focused instructions** — specific instructions = faster, better output
520	3. **Appropriate agent for each step** — Sonnet is faster than Opus. Use Opus only for Arya/Sage/Rex nodes.
521	4. **Don't chain more nodes than needed** — 3–5 nodes is the sweet spot. 7+ nodes is usually overkill.
522	5. **Break into multiple smaller pipelines** — instead of one 8-node monster, run two 4-node pipelines sequentially
523

525	
526	## Troubleshooting
527	
528	### Node turns red / error
529	
530	**Symptom:** A node shows a red error icon during a run.
531	
532	**Cause A — Timeout:** The node took longer than 120 seconds.
533	
534	Fix:
535	- Click the failed node to see the error message
536	- Simplify the instructions (break the task into smaller pieces)
537	- Or split the node into two nodes with focused responsibilities
538	
539	**Cause B — Claude CLI error:** The `claude` subprocess returned an error.
540	
541	Fix:
542	```bash
543	# Verify claude CLI works manually
544	claude -p "Say hello" --print
545	# If this fails, the CLI has a problem — re-authenticate:
546	claude login
547	```
548	
549	**Cause C — Empty output:** The node ran but returned nothing useful.
550	
551	Fix: The instructions likely don't direct Claude to produce a concrete deliverable. See "Node Instructions: Bad vs Good" above.
552	
553	---
554	
555	### Circular edge detected
556	
557	**Symptom:** System shows error "Circular dependency detected" when you try to run.
558	
559	**Cause:** You connected nodes in a way that creates a loop (A → B → C → A).
560	
561	**Fix:** Find and remove the circular edge. The system highlights the problematic edge in red. Delete it. Orchestration only supports DAGs (no cycles).
562	
563	---
564	
565	### Disconnected nodes
566	
567	**Symptom:** A node never runs — it stays gray after the run completes.
568	
569	**Cause:** The node has no incoming edges and is not a Start node. It's isolated from the graph.
570	
571	**Fix:** Connect the node to at least one other node. Either draw an edge from a preceding node to it, or delete it if it's not needed.
572	
573	---
574	
575	### Output is meta-commentary instead of content
576	
577	**Symptom:** A node returns "I would write the listing like this: [description of the listing]" instead of the actual listing.
578	
579	**Cause:** Node instructions don't specify that the agent should produce the deliverable directly.
580	
581	**Fix:** Add explicit output format instructions:
582	```
583	Write the listing. Return the listing only. No preamble, no commentary, no explanation.
584	```
585	
586	See "Node Instructions: Bad vs Good" for more examples.
587	
588	---
589	
590	### Context ballooning (slow pipeline)
591	
592	**Symptom:** Later nodes in the pipeline are very slow or timing out.
593	
594	**Cause:** Upstream nodes produced large outputs that all get passed as context to downstream nodes. By node 4 or 5, the context is 20KB+ of text.
595	
596	**Fix:** Add a Summarizer node:
597	```
598	Node 3 (long output) → Summarizer ("Condense to 5 key points, max 200 words") → Node 4
599	```
600	
601	---
602	
603	### Save not persisting
604	
605	**Symptom:** You save a pipeline, close Claude Hub, reopen it, and the pipeline is gone.
606	
607	**Cause:** Write permission issue on `orchestrations.json`.
608	
609	**Fix:**
610	```bash
611	ls -l "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/orchestrations.json"
612	# If not writable:
613	chmod 644 "/Users/yashbaldha/Desktop/Boldteq App/claude-hub/orchestrations.json"
614	```
615	
616	---
617	
618	### SSE events not streaming (run panel shows nothing)
619	
620	**Symptom:** You click Run, nothing happens in the run panel. After a long wait, maybe an error appears.
621	
622	**Cause:** The SSE connection between the frontend and backend is broken. Often caused by a proxy or browser extension interrupting the connection.
623	
624	**Fix:**
625	1. Check Claude Hub logs: `pm2 logs claude-hub --lines 30`
626	2. Look for errors in the browser console (F12 → Console)
627	3. Try a hard reload: Cmd+Shift+R
628	4. If pm2 shows errors: `pm2 restart claude-hub` then reload the page

3	This guide covers everything you need to do when starting a new project or onboarding an existing one. By the end, Claude Code will know about the project, your agents will have context, slash commands will be available, and the SDK will be wired up.

6	
7	## Why Setup Matters
8	
9	A new project without proper setup means:
10	- Claude Code has no knowledge of the stack, patterns, or decisions
11	- No repeatable commands — you re-explain the same workflow every session
12	- No SDK access — you can't call agents programmatically
13	- Claude Hub doesn't know the project exists — no dashboard, no agent management
14	
15	A properly setup project means:
16	- Claude Code opens with full context on the first message
17	- `/feature`, `/fix`, `/review` work immediately
18	- `callAgent('koda', 'build X')` works from any script
19	- The project appears in Claude Hub with all agents and commands visible

22	
23	## Step 1 — Create the Project's CLAUDE.md
24	
25	### Why this matters
26	
27	The project-level `CLAUDE.md` at the project root is read by Claude Code when that project is open. It supplements the global `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` with project-specific context: exact stack versions, folder structure, architecture decisions, and patterns specific to this codebase.
28	
29	Without it, Claude Code builds on generic assumptions. With it, Claude Code knows exactly what `authenticate.admin(request)` means, what your Prisma models look like, and what your quality standards are.

44	- Bundler: [if applicable]
45	- Node: [minimum version]

## COMPREHENSIVE CLAUDE HUB DOCUMENTATION AUDIT

### DOCUMENTATION COVERAGE SUMMARY

**docs/00-overview.md:**

### FEATURES/ENDPOINTS NOT DOCUMENTED OR UNDER-DOCUMENTED

#### A. MAJOR UNDER-DOCUMENTED OR MISSING FEATURES

1. **AI Chat Assistant Feature (AiAssistant.tsx, entire feature not mentioned)**

   - No documentation on `/ai/chat`, `/ai/stream`, `/ai/history` endpoints
   - No documentation on `streamAiChat()`, `saveAiSession()`, `deleteAiSession()` SDK functions
   - This is a major feature with full session history, context awareness, file suggestions, and apply functionality
   - Missing: architecture, use cases, context building, file application workflow

2. **Memory Brain Feature (entirely undocumented)**
   - Docs mention "memory/" directory in overview but never explain the Memory Brain feature
   - `/api/memory` endpoints completely missing from docs

   - The Memory.tsx page is never mentioned in any doc

   - The Documentation page (routes to `/docs`) is not explained
   - No explanation of how docs are served or where they're stored
